text:
Odysseus should sail away quietly, now that he has won.

Instead, he stands on the deck and jeers at the giant.

It is the one mistake in the whole plan, and it is a mistake of pride.

The giant tears the top off a mountain and throws it.

It lands just in front of the ship, and the wave sweeps them back toward the shore.

The crew begs him to stop, because the giant has already thrown one rock at them.

But Odysseus shouts once more, and this time he gives his name.

If anyone asks who blinded you, tell them it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, of Ithaca.

So much for Nobody.

The giant answers that a prophet named Tell-ih-muss once warned him that Odysseus would take his eye.

He had expected a great warrior, and instead he got "a little insignificant weakling."

He offers presents if Odysseus will come back, and Odysseus answers that it will take more than Poseidon to cure that eye.

Then the giant lifts both hands toward the sky, and prays to Poseidon.

Never let Odysseus reach his home, he asks.

Or if he must, let him come "late and in sore plight, after losing all his men."

Poseidon listens.

The prayer is answered, and the rest of the Odyssey is the answer.

It will be years before Odysseus sees Ithaca again.
